The Blackhawks Week That Was and Will Be, 10/7: Exhale

Deep breaths after Chicago’s first win of the season.

Posted on October 7, 2026October 7, 2026 by Dave Melton
(Photo by Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire)

Now the season really begins.

There can be a bit of a rush — too much of one, sometimes — to assign bigger meanings to the first few games of the hockey season because of how long it’s been since we’ve had relevant games to discuss. This lengthy Blackhawks’ rebuild only exacerbates this feeling, because what’s being built here still has so many questions surrounding it, yet we’ve never been closer to getting some of those answers.

Some breaking news here: over the course of a now 84-game season, there are going to be wins and there are going to be losses. Shocking, right? So, adequate data from both sets of samples are necessary before a true pictures of what’s happening on the ice can be painted, otherwise what comes into focus won’t be correct. It was fair to have Chicago’s first three games raise red flags, though, because the struggles noted during those games were so similar to the struggles noted so often last season. It certainly could have gone worse, though: just ask Philadelphia!

Still, the manner in which teams win games can be just as telling as how they lose them. Take that initial Blackhawks win of the season as an example of it. The Hawks had the better of play for much of the first two periods but were completely overwhelmed by the Blues in the third. The support of a few posts, a few big Spencer Knights saves and a few empty-net goals were all essential in securing that win. If the Hawks victories consistently feel more like an escape with two points instead of a more sound, solid performance to earn them, then we’ll need to see why that happens. It’s hard to make any bold conclusions right now with only one such victory to dissect.

One thing to keep an eye on over this initial chunk of games without Connor Bedard, though, is that his absence hasn’t necessarily spelled doom for this team in the past. It did during the 2023-24 season, when Bedard missed 14 games and the team went 3-10-1 with some dismal possession numbers. Last season, though, Bedard missed 12 games between December and January and the Hawks went 5-6-1 while outperforming much of their 5-on-5 numbers through the season. Here’s how the current stretch compares with those two others:

  • 2023-24 season: 3-10-1 record, 45.18 CF%, 45.73 CF%, 44.66 xGF%, 42.35 SCF%, 40.61 HDCF%, outscored 31-14 (31.11 GF%) during 5-on-5 play
  • 2025-26 season: 5-6-1, 50.57 CF%, 47.35 SF%, 49.12 xGF%, 49.80 SCF%, 45.13 HDCF%, outscored 31-21 (40.38 GF%) during 5-on-5 play
  • 2026-27 season: 1-3-0, 39.39 CF%, 37.72 SF%, 34.55 xGF%, 37.02 SCF%, 36.11 HDCF%, outscored 11-6 (35.29 GF%) during 5-on-5 play

The numbers still look dismal overall for the Hawks to start this season, with them battling for the battle three spots in most of those categories with either the San Jose Sharks or the aforementioned Flyers. We’ll see how much Bedard’s increasingly imminent return will affect things, because that is one possible saving grace from what we’ve seen so far, even if this team hasn’t always suffered as much without him.

Hold Up a Light

I should probably have a better word for it than this, but “weird” is the one that keeps landing on my tongue whenever I’ve talked about watching Patrick Kane return to the Blackhawks this season. Tuesday’s game raised that thought to its highest levels, as so much of the fanfare before, during and after the game. I fully understand why some people are so excited about it and I’m not going to talk you out of those feelings even if I’m not sharing them.

There are probably two reasons for all of this: the first is that it felt like we did the Patrick Kane farewell tour three years ago, making peace with the fact that the golden era we all enjoyed so much was reaching its official end on the ice, even if the realization that those years were firmly in the past had settled in long before his March 2023 departure because of how far south the team had plummeted in the standings. There was no reason to assume Kane was ever coming back to the Hawks again — and, given the condition of his hip at the time, it was fair to conclude that Kane’s entire hockey career on its last legs. While this version of Kane seems to have plenty of NHL-level play left in it, there’s also the realization that it’s not quite the version of Kane that was averaged over a point per game for this initial 15-plus regular seasons. He has one goal in four games so far this season, which is certainly affected by the collectively subpar performance of this team but also points to this version of Kane not being as able to outperform his team’s shortcomings as the prior versions of him could.

The other reason is that Kane’s run in Chicago was so heavily tied to moments that featured so many other players as well, which is part of the reason why that team was so dominant in its heyday. Having two of those players watching from a UC suite in street clothes while Kane was playing with a completely different roster around him underscores this contrast even more. It’s like seeing a band several years down the road on a reunion tour that features the same lead singer but with replacement acts behind every other instrument on the stage. They may look the same and they may be playing the same song, but it just doesn’t sound the same.

There are 80 games left this season with another year on Kane’s contract following this one, so perhaps those feelings subside before this chapter of his career is written. For this initial stretch, though, it’s still just … weird.
